clue.text: Peter, for one, if rejected by an American general

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the little word if is read backwards

parts.note: William Tecumseh Sherman was a Union general in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A biblical Peter is turned down by a US army general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns IF into FI. Saint Peter was a fisher on the Sea of Galilee before becoming an apostle.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle Peter caught fish for a living, so he is an example of an angler by trade.

clue.text: Aircraft carrying troops to a commercial vessel

indicators.note: carrying means the aircraft holds the troops inside

parts.note: a fighter is a combat aircraft
RE are the Royal Engineers, British army troops

explanation.surface: A plane takes soldiers to a merchant ship.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for the Royal Engineers is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A cargo ship that carries goods for trade is a commercial vessel.

clue.text: Odds on renegade being caught by 1 ac

parts.note: SP is the starting price, the betting odds in a race
a rat is a turncoat or deserter

explanation.surface: Betting on a traitor being caught by the angler.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 across is FISHERMAN, so the definition is a fish he might catch. SP for starting price is a racing term.
explanation.definitionFit: A small herring-like fish is the sort of catch a man with a rod or net lands.

clue.text: Continental characters on a rupee

indicators.note: characters means the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Foreign lettering printed on an Indian coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' signals that the letters of ON A RUPEE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Continental in British usage means from mainland Europe, as opposed to Britain.

clue.text: Class represented by three MA's and one student

indicators.note: represented by means the letters below are reworked into a new form

parts.note: three copies of MA
I is the Roman numeral for one
L is a learner driver's plate, so a student

explanation.surface: A university group made up of three graduates and one undergraduate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented by' rearranges MAMAMA plus I and L.
explanation.definitionFit: In biological taxonomy this is the class of all warm-blooded animals that suckle young.

clue.text: Anglo-Saxon sign found in north-east near a battleground

indicators.note: found in means the first piece sits within the abbreviation for north-east

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east
AS is the conventional symbol for Anglo-Saxon
by means near, as in standing by

explanation.surface: Old English lettering discovered in the north-east close to a field of combat.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1645 Battle of Naseby in Northamptonshire was a decisive English Civil War battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Northamptonshire village gave its name to a key Civil War fight, so it is a site of battle.

clue.text: In our case hundreds are present

definitions.note: a plural verb phrase; the answer is the matching verb, as in 'they ... '

indicators.note: case here acts as a verb, the word our encasing what follows it

parts.note: taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so two hundreds give CC

explanation.surface: In our particular situation, hundreds of people turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb 'case' puts CC inside OUR; 'In' at the front is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To happen or exist in a place is to be there, so the verb swaps for being present.

clue.text: Error ruined youngster's first model of the planets

indicators.note: ruined means the letters of error are wrecked into a new order
first means only the opening letter of youngster is taken

explanation.surface: A child's mistake spoils a scale replica of the solar system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' makes ORRER from ERROR.
explanation.definitionFit: A clockwork device showing the planets orbiting the sun is a mechanical model of them.

clue.text: Prepare to discharge fish — it's unwelcome in the kitchen

parts.note: to cock a gun is to make it ready to fire
a roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Getting ready to throw out a fish that is not wanted in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cook discarding fish; the definition is a household pest.
explanation.definitionFit: A scuttling insect pest infesting larders is the last visitor any cook wants.

clue.text: Establishes contact, though not by such circulars

explanation.surface: Making contact by phone rather than by posted leaflets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circulars' suggests mailshots; here it means circular objects, loops.
explanation.definitionFit: To phone someone is to call them; round loops are hoops or bands.

clue.text: As an aid to communication it can't be beaten

definitions.text: As an aid to communication it can't be beaten

parts.words: As an aid to communication it can't be beaten
parts.note: reads like praise for an unbeatable gadget, but the hearing membrane is in fact beaten by every sound wave

explanation.surface: Boasting of a communication device that nothing can better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can't be beaten' sounds like 'is unbeatable', but the joke is that this part of the ear is literally struck by sound all the time.
explanation.definitionFit: The tympanic membrane vibrates with sound, letting us hear speech, so it aids communication.

clue.text: It introduces competition new to an old nomad

indicators.note: introduces means comes in front of, so the piece for It leads the piece for competition

parts.note: it is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a race is a competition

explanation.surface: Something presents a contest that is unfamiliar to an ancient wanderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' meaning sex appeal (SA) is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Saracens were the desert Arab peoples of the Roman era, wandering tribes of Syria and Arabia.

clue.text: Climb in striking costume

explanation.surface: Scaling a peak while wearing an eye-catching outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise or ascend is to climb; as a noun, it is slang for an outfit, often a showy one.

clue.text: Perfume ingredient — yellowish in England, grey in France

parts.note: amber is the English word for a yellowish orange colour
gris is French for grey

explanation.surface: A scent component described by its colour in two languages.
explanation.definitionFit: This waxy substance from sperm whales has long been used to fix the scent in perfumes.

clue.text: Land around Portishead for one of Remus's brothers?

indicators.note: around means the word for land is placed about the other piece

parts.note: terrain is land or ground
read as 'Port is head', the head of Port is its first letter P

explanation.surface: Ground near the Somerset town of Portishead is offered for a relative of Remus.
explanation.walkthrough: Portishead is a town near Bristol, but read 'Port is head' it gives P. Remus is Uncle Remus, whose tales feature Brer (brother) Rabbit, Brer Fox and Brer Terrapin.
explanation.definitionFit: Brer Terrapin is a character in the Uncle Remus stories, where animals are titled 'Brer', meaning brother.

clue.text: The contrite aren't uncommonly shut up inside

definitions.note: a noun phrase for sorry people; the answer is the adjective used as a noun

indicators.note: inside means the piece for shut up goes within the jumbled letters
uncommonly means the letters of aren't are put in an unusual order

parts.note: pent, as in pent-up, means shut in

explanation.surface: Sorry people are unusually confined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' makes REANT from AREN'T, and 'inside' puts PENT within it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sorry for wrongdoing is to be penitent, so the remorseful are the penitent.

clue.text: Satire loses nothing on becoming light

indicators.note: loses means letters are taken away from the word for satire

parts.note: a lampoon is a satirical attack
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A satirical piece that, stripped of everything, becomes trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes O and ON from LAMPOON; 'becoming' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp is a device that gives illumination, so it can stand for a light.

clue.text: Outline of old poem written in prison cell

indicators.note: written in means the poem is placed inside the cell

parts.note: peter is old slang for a prison cell
rime is an archaic spelling of rhyme, as in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: Draft of a poem composed while imprisoned.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER is criminal slang for a cell or safe.
explanation.definitionFit: The boundary round a shape is its outline or border.

clue.text: Sequel to Hood's month of privation?

definitions.text: Sequel to Hood's month of privation?

parts.words: Sequel to Hood's month of privation?
parts.note: Thomas Hood's poem lists the absences of the eleventh month, no sun, no moon, so the one after follows it

explanation.surface: Asking what follows a poet's month of hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood's poem 'No!' ends 'No fruits, no flowers, no leaves, no birds, November!', so the month of privation is November and the sequel the month after.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelfth month follows the eleventh, which Hood made a month of nothing.

clue.text: Timekeeper with tail — Cerberus for one

parts.note: a watch keeps time
to tail someone is to dog, follow, them

explanation.surface: A clock with a tail compared to the dog of Hades.
explanation.walkthrough: Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the underworld in Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerberus guarded the gates of Hades, a mythical guard hound.

clue.text: Cable when old may result in money

definitions.text: Cable when old may result in money

parts.words: Cable when old may result in money
parts.note: plays on the saying money for old cord, meaning pay for easy work

explanation.surface: Worn-out wiring that might somehow earn you cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money for old rope' is a British idiom for easy, undeserved earnings.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable is a thick cord, and the British idiom pairs old cord with easy money.

clue.text: Satisfied Herbert with alternative writing device

parts.note: met as in met a demand, satisfied it
A. P. Herbert, the British humorist, signed his Punch pieces APH
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Content that Herbert chose a different literary tool.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert was a British writer and MP known by his initials APH.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech that calls one thing another is a tool used in writing.

clue.text: The shrewd part of Seneca's tutelage

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Clever folk learnt from the Roman philosopher's teaching.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrewd and sharp-witted mean the same; the adjective stands for the clever as a group.

clue.text: Chinese society members once seen in 8

explanation.surface: Members of an old Chinese secret society appearing in boxing rings.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boxers were a Chinese secret society behind the 1900 uprising; 8 down is RINGS, where fighters box.
explanation.definitionFit: The Righteous Harmony Society were called Boxers in English; fighters in the ring are pugilists.

clue.text: Rock is not as dense maybe? Not quite

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not quite means the last letter of the final word is missing

explanation.surface: Asking whether a stone is less compact, and answering not really.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' drops the E of 'dense', leaving NOT AS DENS, which 'maybe' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedimentary stone formed from compressed grains is a kind of rock.

clue.text: Made one cry stinking fish, did it?

definitions.text: Made one cry stinking fish, did it?

parts.words: Made one cry stinking fish, did it?
parts.note: asks whether a fish gave off an odour strong enough to bring tears, combining the fish and the past tense of to smell

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a rotten fish brought tears to the eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a small fish and the British past tense of 'smell'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small silvery fish shares its name with the past tense of give off an odour.

clue.text: Attractiveness rare at first in an autocrat

indicators.note: in means the first letter goes inside the word for the ruler

parts.note: cham is an archaic form of khan, an absolute ruler

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of rare is used

explanation.surface: Charisma is a rare quality in a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAM, an old spelling of khan, is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Charm is the quality of being pleasing or appealing, a synonym for allure.

clue.text: A price to pay for Bikini, perhaps

parts.note: a toll is a charge paid, as on a road or bridge

explanation.surface: The cost of buying a swimsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Bikini is a Pacific coral island, used for nuclear tests, which gave the swimsuit its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands is a ring-shaped coral reef island.

clue.text: Time, certainly, for an end to clerical error

parts.note: an era is a period of time
sure as in 'sure!', meaning certainly

explanation.surface: Insisting that now is definitely the moment to stop office mistakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbing out a word removes a written mistake, ending a clerk's slip.

clue.text: A pillar of support for the retired

definitions.text: A pillar of support for the retired

parts.words: A pillar of support for the retired
parts.note: reads as a backer of pensioners, but the retired are simply people gone to bed

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who helps elderly pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' suggests pensioners; here it means having gone to bed for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Each upright at a corner of a bedstead is a post holding up a sleeper.

clue.text: Sports championship? Right

explanation.surface: Asking whether a sports trophy is deserved.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion holds the crown in a sport; a legal claim to property is also called this.

clue.text: Stray disturbed arrest outside horse pound

indicators.note: outside means the jumbled letters go around the other pieces
disturbed means the letters of arrest are jumbled

parts.note: gee-gee, GG, is a child's word for a horse
L stands for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A roaming animal is upset by being detained beside the animal pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' makes STRAER from ARREST, and 'outside' puts it around GGL.
explanation.definitionFit: One who strays or wanders off from the group is a laggard.
